opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's going to shift quite a lot. In the early days, a lot of companies came to open source almost for experimentation. It was free, you could download a model and play with it, and you didn't have to sign a big contract to find out whether this AI thing was useful for you at all. The entry ticket was very low.

As the market matures, I think the reasons become much more strategic. The first one is control. Once AI is not a side project but sits at the core of your product, you really want to own that piece of your stack. You don't want your roadmap to depend on whether a provider deprecates a model, changes its behavior overnight, or raises prices. With open weights, you can pin a version, and it behaves the same way tomorrow as it does today. For a lot of enterprises that predictability matters a lot.

The second is data and privacy. Many companies have very sensitive data, in healthcare, finance, the public sector, and they want to run models on their own infrastructure, sometimes fully on-premise, sometimes on device. Open models make that possible in a way that's hard to match otherwise.

The third, which I think will become the most important, is specialization. The general-purpose frontier models are amazing, but when you have a very specific task you do millions of times a day, a smaller open model fine-tuned on your own data is often better, faster, and much cheaper. As companies get more sophisticated, they realize they don't need a giant model for everything. They need the right model for each task, and they want to be able to shape it themselves. That's where open source really shines, because you can actually go inside the model, adapt it, distill it, and build on the work of the whole community.

And then there's a more long-term point about understanding and trust. When you can inspect the weights, and ideally the training data and recipes too, you can audit what the model does, study its failure modes, and build real confidence in it. As regulation develops and companies become accountable for what their AI systems do, being able to look inside the box will be a big advantage.

So I'd summarize it as a move from "open source because it's free and easy to try" to "open source because it gives me control, customization, and trust over something that has become core to my business." That's a much more durable reason, and I think it's why open models will keep a very large share of real-world deployments, even if the very top of the frontier is sometimes held by closed models.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized open models can be cheaper, but does not state that cost savings will become a more important adoption reason than they are today.

r002.rationale: The response gives current and expected reasons for adoption, but does not identify developing capabilities that do not yet exist as a current reason.

r003.rationale: It predicts greater emphasis on control and running models on company infrastructure, but does not clearly say that owning the full stack on which models run will become more important.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the reasons are going to shift quite a lot, and honestly they already have started to.

In the early phase, the main reason people came to open models was cost, and maybe a bit of curiosity. You could download Llama or Mistral or one of the Qwen models, run it on your own hardware, and avoid paying per token to a closed API. That's a real motivation, but it's also a fragile one, because closed API prices keep falling. If your only reason for going open is that it's cheaper, you're always one price cut away from switching back.

What I see happening as the market matures is that the motivations become much more structural. The first one is control. When you build a product on a closed model, you're building on something that can change under you. The provider updates the model, the behavior shifts, your prompts stop working the way they did, and you have no recourse. With an open model, you pin a version, you own the weights, and that thing behaves the same way in five years. For companies putting AI into production systems, that stability matters more than people initially realize.

The second one is customization. Fine-tuning, distillation, adding your own data, taking a model and making it really good at your specific domain rather than good at everything. You simply cannot do that deeply with a closed model. And as companies move from demos to actual products, they discover that a smaller model specialized on their problem often beats a huge general model, and it's cheaper and faster on top of that.

The third one, and I think this becomes the dominant reason over time, is sovereignty in a broad sense. Not just governments, although that's part of it, but companies in regulated industries, companies with sensitive data, companies in Europe or Asia who don't want their core technology to depend on two or three American providers. Open models let you run things where your data is, under your rules, and understand what the model was trained on. That transparency piece gets more important as regulation comes in.

And then there's a more subtle shift. Early on, open source was seen as the follower, always six months to a year behind the frontier. As the gap closes, and in some areas it already has, the question stops being "is open good enough" and becomes "why would I give up control for a marginal capability difference I may not even need." At that point, open becomes the default for most use cases, and closed models become the thing you reach for in specific situations, rather than the other way around.

So the short version: we go from "it's cheaper" to "it's the only way I can build something I actually own." That's a much more durable reason, and it's the one that makes me confident this isn't just a phase.

r001.rationale: The response says cost is an early motivation that will give way to more structural reasons, so it does not predict cost savings will become more important.

r002.rationale: It mentions curiosity as an early motivation, but does not identify developing capabilities that do not yet exist as a current reason.

r003.rationale: It discusses owning model weights and controlling where models run, but does not predict that ownership of the full stack on which models run will become more important.

astra-6.text:
I think the reasons will shift from experimentation to control. Today, a lot of companies use open-source AI because they want to try things, understand how the models work, and customize them. As the market matures, the question becomes: how much of this technology do you want to depend on somebody else for?

If AI becomes a core part of your product, you care about being able to run it where you need to, adapt it to your data, and keep using it without a provider changing the terms or retiring a model. Cost also becomes more important as you move from a demo to serving millions of requests.

So I don’t think every company will choose open source for everything. There will be a mix. But the motivation becomes less about trying the latest model and more about owning the capabilities that matter to your business.

r001.rationale: It says cost becomes more important when companies move from demos to serving millions of requests, indicating it will matter more as adoption matures.

r002.rationale: It names experimentation, understanding models, and customization as current reasons, but does not say companies are developing capabilities that do not yet exist.

r003.rationale: It predicts greater control over deployment and continued use, but does not identify ownership of the full stack running the models as a reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reasons will become much more practical. Early on, companies might choose open source because they believe in it, or because they want to experiment with the technology. As the market matures, they’ll ask: What gives me the best performance for my use case, at the right cost, with the control I need?

That’s where open source becomes very compelling. You can adapt a model to your own data, run it within your infrastructure, and avoid depending entirely on one provider. You don’t necessarily need the largest model for every task. A smaller, specialized model can be a better fit.

So I expect the conversation to move from “Do we support open source?” to “Does this help us build a better product?” And companies will probably use a mixture of open and closed models, depending on what they need.

r001.rationale: The response mentions choosing a model at the right cost, but does not say cost savings will become more important as the market matures.

r002.rationale: It mentions experimenting with the technology as an early reason, but does not identify developing capabilities that do not yet exist.

r003.rationale: It mentions running models within company infrastructure and having control, but does not predict that owning the full stack will become a more important reason.
